text: 16,17 cholelithiasis and cholestasis have been reported, with the latter sometimes progressing to liver failure.18 Although the aetiology is consid- ered multifactorial,18 contamination of the solution with manga- nese (see Accumulation under Adverse Effects of Manganese, p.1956) or aluminium19 has been suggested as one possible cause of the cholestasis. Aluminium toxicity has also been implicated in the osteomalacia seen in patients on long-term parenteral nutrition.3,17 Osteopenia and osteoporosis have also been reported;17 possible mecha- nisms include calcium, phosphate, or magnesium deficiencies, vitamin D deficiency or toxicity, vitamin K deficiency, or exces- sive protein.3 A review, however, considered the risk to be mini- mal, with little deleterious effect on cortical bone and an im- provement on trabecular bone.5 Other factors implicated in possible metabolic bone disease include calcium deficiency and vitamin D toxicity.17 Other metabolic complications associated with parenteral nutri- tion include hyperglycaemia, hypoglycaemia, hyperlipidaemia, hypercapnia, acid–base disturbances, and ‘refeeding syn- drome’.20 Hyperglycaemia may be due to excessive glucose in- fusion, and can lead to immunodepression and an increased risk of infection; insulin therapy is indicated if it persists. Hypogly- caemia, although less common, may occur if parenteral nutrition is interrupted or as a result of an insulin overdose. Hyperlipidae- mia is caused by excessive fatty acid synthesis from glucose, or impaired lipid clearance. The use of a mixture of medium-chain and long-chain triglycerides (rather than long-chain triglyceride emulsions alone) may result in fewer serum lipid abnormalities since medium-chain triglycerides are oxidised faster than long- chain triglycerides. Overfeeding of total calories and glucose can lead to hypercapnia which can cause acute respiratory acidosis.20 While most acid–base disturbances are related to the underlying condition, excess chloride or acetate in the parenteral nutrition solution may cause metabolic acidosis or alkalosis, respective- ly.17 The ‘refeeding syndrome’ can occur when severely mal- nourished patients are given rapid nutritional repletion, leading to fluid and electrolyte imbalances, glucose intolerance, and vi- tamin deficiencies. These may result in significant or even fatal cardiac, pulmonary, renal, gastrointestinal, and neuromuscular complications. Electrolyte disturbances include sodium reten- tion, hypophosphataemia, hypokalaemia, and hypomagnesae- mia; thiamine deficiency may lead to Wernicke’s encephalopa- thy in malnourished patients or in thiamine-deficient patients given high carbohydrate loads.20 1.
